nodes.label: Sensemaking in Multi-Agent LLM Interfaces Study
nodes.rationale: Design-led qualitative study exploring how users interpret and evaluate transparency in multi-agent LLMs through five interface variants across information-seeking and reasoning tasks.

nodes.label: Multi-Agent Interface Design Space
nodes.rationale: Seven design dimensions: Agent Composition, Role Specialisation, Response Format, Disagreement & Critique, Interaction Topology, Information Flow, Output Aggregation.

nodes.label: V1: Final Answer Interface
nodes.rationale: Shows only aggregated final decision with no agent-level visibility; represents opaque system output baseline.

nodes.label: V2: Agents Answer Interface
nodes.rationale: Displays individual agent responses and majority vote count without rationales; provides surface-level transparency.

nodes.label: V3: Agents Explain Interface
nodes.rationale: Shows individual agent responses with brief rationales and aggregated final answer; strikes balance between transparency and cognitive load.

nodes.label: V4: Agents Critique Interface
nodes.rationale: Introduces dedicated critic agent who evaluates each agent's response, followed by summarised final answer; shows system self-checking.

nodes.label: V5: Agents Debate Interface
nodes.rationale: Presents multi-turn inter-agent discussion where initially disagreeing agents deliberate and converge on consensus answer; mirrors human-like deliberation.

nodes.label: Goldilocks Zone of Transparency
nodes.rationale: Context-sensitive 'just right' level of process visibility that balances informational value against cognitive workload; dynamic threshold shaped by task, interface, and user characteristics.

nodes.label: Ensemble Size as Reliability Signal
nodes.rationale: Users interpret number of agents as proxy for system capability and reliability; larger ensembles perceived as more credible but introduce cognitive trade-offs.

nodes.label: Agent-Level Rationales Support Sensemaking
nodes.rationale: Brief agent explanations enable users to weigh competing reasoning paths, scaffold own decision-making, and retain agency; without rationales, majority heuristic dominates.

nodes.label: Disagreement as Double-Edged Cue
nodes.rationale: Unexplained disagreement erodes trust; explained disagreement with rationales helps explore competing perspectives and refine reasoning; critic agent enhances perceived trustworthiness.

nodes.label: Progressive Disclosure for Transparency
nodes.rationale: Eight of twelve participants preferred flexible, on-demand transparency with collapsible interface elements; allows access to rationales only when needed without default cognitive burden.

nodes.label: Task Complexity Shapes Transparency Needs
nodes.rationale: Simple information-seeking tasks prefer minimal transparency (V1, V2); complex reasoning tasks benefit from process visibility (V4, V5); overly elaborate outputs in simple tasks backfire.

nodes.label: User Expertise Influences Transparency Preferences
nodes.rationale: High task domain expertise correlates with preference for minimal transparency; low confidence increases need for visible reasoning; dispositional trust shapes information sufficiency judgements.

nodes.label: User Mental Models of Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.rationale: Users employ metaphors (panels, teams, expert systems) and anthropomorphise agents; some infer aggregation mechanisms (voting, probability); model/vendor identity serves as reliability heuristic.

nodes.label: Majority Agreement Heuristic
nodes.rationale: Visible majority agreement strongly enhances perceived reliability; users frequently disregard minority agents; reflects bandwagon effect but may mislead when majority is incorrect.

nodes.label: Comparative Structured Observation Methodology
nodes.rationale: Design-led qualitative method where participants compare and reflect on interface variants; card-sorting activities elicit fine-grained insights into transparency and trustworthiness judgements.

nodes.label: Transparency as Contextual Sufficiency
nodes.rationale: Reconceptualises transparency not as volume dial but as sufficiency judgement; users seek enough insight for decision-making without overwhelming cognitive load; fit matters more than quantity.

nodes.label: Epistemic Signals in Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.rationale: Disagreement, critique, consensus, and diverse rationales function as user-facing transparency cues; each is double-edged with benefits and risks depending on presentation and context.

nodes.label: Critic Agent Effect on Trust
nodes.rationale: Dedicated critic agent boosts perceived trustworthiness by signalling system self-checking; provides scaffolding for user reasoning; can backfire if perceived as highlighting system limitations.

nodes.label: Task Selection: Information-Seeking vs. Reasoning
nodes.rationale: Binary general-knowledge questions (information-seeking) vs. LSAT logical reasoning questions (reasoning); reflect common real-world LLM use cases with varying complexity and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Interaction Topology (Design Dimension D5)
nodes.rationale: How agents interact (parallel vs. sequential); did not emerge as salient cue shaping user transparency or trust judgements in study.

nodes.label: Information Flow Architecture (Design Dimension D6)
nodes.rationale: Pipeline vs. hierarchical information flow; remained perceptually latent and did not function as user-facing trustworthiness signal.

nodes.label: Consensus Through Debate Mechanism
nodes.rationale: Multi-turn inter-agent discussion reaching consensus; perceived as trustworthy and thorough but sometimes introduces unnecessary complexity for simple tasks.

nodes.label: Multi-Agent Study Participant Sample
nodes.rationale: 12 participants (6 men, 6 women) with diverse educational backgrounds and AI familiarity; most frequent LLM users; varied dispositional trust and AI literacy.

nodes.label: Card-Sorting Activity for Transparency Assessment
nodes.rationale: Participants arranged interface variant cards along spectrums for perceived transparency, helpfulness, and reliability; elicited comparative reasoning and trade-offs.

nodes.label: Reflexive Thematic Analysis Approach
nodes.rationale: Braun and Clarke six-phase approach; deductive and inductive coding; dynamic codebook refined through team collaboration.
